tier_reason: The second benchmark meets all four Tier A conditions. (1) The code is public. The page https://qlibs.github.io/mph/perfect_hashing is perfect_hashing/index.html on the qlibs/mph 'benchmark' branch, served by GitHub Pages from that branch root. It is the rendered export of perfect_hashing/benchmark.ipynb. The harness is in the same folder: Makefile, Dockerfile, benchmark.hpp, and one .cpp per target (mph.cpp, unordered_map.cpp, map.cpp, boost_unordered_flat_map.cpp, frozen.cpp, gperf.cpp, if_else.cpp, switch_case.cpp). The qlibs.github.io repo is only the org landing page and holds no benchmark code. (2) The CPU is stated: the notebook prints /proc/cpuinfo showing '12th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-12650H'. Runs are pinned to CPU 1 with taskset. (3) Flags are stated: CXXFLAGS='-std=c++20 -DNDEBUG -O3 -march=native' is set in the notebook and printed on every plot title. The Makefile adds -DNTEST and the constexpr/template-depth limits. (4) The compiler is stated: the page and plots say clang++-19 and g++-13. The committed Makefile sets CXX=clang++-18 unconditionally, and a makefile assignment overrides the CXX environment variable the notebook passes. So both columns were most likely built with clang++-18. The byte-identical stripped binary sizes in the 'clang++-19' and 'g++-13' panels (int_to_int and str_to_int) support this. The compiler actually used is still fixed by public code, so the run is reproducible and stays Tier A. The per-compiler labels are unreliable (see caveats). This supersedes the earlier Tier C, which rested on the README nanobench tables that give no compiler version and no CPU.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Perfect-hashing benchmark on an i7-12650H with -O3 -march=native. The page shows plots only, so all values below were read off the plot pixels (derived from page data, about ±1 px). Plotted time is the total for size×100,000 lookups. 1024 string keys of length 1-8, all hits: std::unordered_map ~2.14 s vs mph ~0.16 s ('clang++-19' panel), ~13.7x (~21 ns vs ~1.5 ns per lookup); 'g++-13' panel ~2.07 s vs ~0.15 s, ~14x. In the same run gperf ~0.46 s (~2.9x slower than mph), boost::unordered_flat_map ~0.91 s (~5.9x) and frozen ~1.44 s (~9.2x). 1024 string keys of length exactly 8, all hits: std::unordered_map ~1.58 s vs mph ~0.15 s, ~10x; gperf ~2.1x slower than mph. 1024 uint32 keys, all hits: std::unordered_map ~0.76 s vs mph ~0.13 s, ~5.8-6.1x; boost::unordered_flat_map ~1.15-1.3x; frozen ~2.1-2.3x. 32 string keys of length 1-8, all hits: std::unordered_map ~0.052 s vs mph ~0.0033 s, ~15x (low precision because mph sits near the axis floor). mph is not faster everywhere. All misses, 1024 string keys: gperf ~0.11 s beats mph ~0.13 s. All misses, 1024 int keys: boost::unordered_flat_map roughly ties mph (~0.14 s each in the 'g++-13' panel). std::unordered_map is slower than mph in every plot. The README nanobench tables (no CPU stated) are unchanged: std::unordered_map 15.32 ns vs mph 1.58 ns at 100 keys of length 8 (~9.7x).
corrections.baseline: std::unordered_map (std::hash), std::map, boost::unordered_flat_map (Boost 1.85), frozen::unordered_map, gperf, if-else and switch-case chains
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Page labels say clang++-19 and g++-13 with -std=c++20 -DNDEBUG -O3 -march=native. The Makefile also adds -DNTEST -fconstexpr-steps=1000000000 -ftemplate-depth=1024 and -I for Boost 1.85. Both columns were most likely built with clang++-18, because the committed Makefile hard-codes CXX=clang++-18, which overrides the notebook's CXX environment variable. The stripped binary sizes are identical in both panels. The Dockerfile also installs clang 18 and gcc 13.
corrections.hardware: 12th Gen Intel Core i7-12650H (from /proc/cpuinfo in the notebook). Pinned to logical CPU 1 (a P-core) with taskset. Turbo Boost was on and the intel_pstate governor was powersave: pyperf system tune failed with permission errors.
corrections.workload: Lookups in static maps whose keys are known at compile time. int_to_int: uint16-range keys with 1-32 entries, and uint32-range keys with 1-1024 entries. str_to_int: string_view keys of length 1-8 or exactly 8, with 1-32 and 1-1024 entries. Hit probability 1.0, 0.5 and 0.0. Each target is a separate binary that times size×100,000 lookups from a pre-generated vector (std::chrono total, median of 3 runs). Checksums are asserted equal across all targets. Baselines: std::map, std::unordered_map (std::hash), boost::unordered_flat_map, frozen::unordered_map, gperf (string keys only), and if_else/switch_case chains. Build time and stripped binary size are also plotted. Harness: https://github.com/qlibs/mph/tree/benchmark/perfect_hashing. The README nanobench tables (5-100 keys) remain as secondary first-party data.
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark by the mph author, run 2024-07-02. Results are shown only as plots; every number was read off the plot pixels (derived from page data). The compiler labels are unreliable: the Makefile's hard-coded CXX=clang++-18 overrides the notebook's CXX, and the binary sizes in the 'clang++-19' and 'g++-13' panels are identical, so this is almost certainly one compiler (likely clang++-18), not a clang vs gcc comparison. baseline_stdlib libstdc++ is inferred: Linux/Ubuntu, and no -stdlib=libc++ appears anywhere. Reproducibility gaps: the benchmark branch does not vendor the mph header (-I.. points at a branch root with no 'mph' file), so the mph version must be supplied by hand (about v5.0.0 / main 2e9418c at run time). frozen and gperf versions are not stated. Key sets come from Python's unseeded random, and only the C++ lookup stream is seeded. Timing is noisy: turbo on, powersave governor, non-monotonic std::unordered_map curves. Plotted time includes streaming a size×100k-element lookup vector, so mph's ~1.5 ns per lookup at 1024 keys may be close to a memory-streaming floor. mph is not fastest in miss-heavy runs: gperf beats it on 1024 string keys at 0% hits, and boost::unordered_flat_map ties it on 1024 int keys at 0% hits. The README's std::unordered_map-with-boost::hash caveat applies only to the README tables, since this harness uses std::hash. Ratios of ~6-15x vs std::unordered_map are plausible for small static sets under -O3.
